Purpose and interpretation

The full-system correction improves coverage over plain IF in several weak- information conditions, but at a substantial and sometimes extreme width cost. It is not a general replacement for person bootstrap inference. Actual delete-one refits are much more widely available than the analytic methods, yet their symmetric Wald intervals still under-cover in several profiles.

Key fresh findings:

  • Full IF and HC3 each return 756/1,200 analyses. All 444 refusals are the pre-existing singular-measurement gate; there are no additional HC3 sensitivity refusals or driver/API errors. Delete-one returns 1,192/1,200; person percentile returns 1,158/1,200. These are paired structural analyses, not independent measurement-dataset counts.
  • At truth .40, hard-profile HC3 coverage is 86.7–95.8%, versus 71.1–85.9% for plain IF on exactly the same 45–65 eligible datasets/profile. Paired gains are about 10–16 percentage points in low balanced, negative-correlation, small/short and unequal-information profiles; their unadjusted paired MC intervals exclude zero. Low larger-N gains only 3.1 points (MC interval includes zero). These are exploratory comparisons, not multiplicity-adjusted claims.
  • On common HC3/bootstrap datasets, the median ratio of HC3 to bootstrap width is 1.62–1.85 in the hard profiles. HC3’s 95th width percentiles are roughly 8.7–28.0, versus 1.0–1.64 for bootstrap on their respective returned sets. No extreme intervals were capped or removed. Higher HC3 coverage often trades off detection and precision; mean SE alone obscures these tails.
  • Delete-one effect coverage is 81.6–91.9% in hard profiles, with 98–100 returned intervals/profile. Person-percentile coverage is 81.5–96.9%, with 92–98 intervals. The small/short point bias remains −.178 at truth .40; none of the variance methods changes the original coefficient.
  • Analytic deletion shifts closely match actual deletions in the high-reliability control (median focal relative RMSE .012). Among common hard-profile datasets with a singularity/floor/final-branch deletion transition, median relative RMSE ranges .55–1.33. Without those transitions it is about .027–.201. These selected-subset diagnostics are consistent with limitations of local deletion approximations; they do not isolate a causal mechanism.
  • All six remote R-platform checks pass. Independent study validation checks all endpoints, actual centered/uncentered covariance formulas, public APIs, fresh inputs, source hashes and B prefixes. Half-step sensitivity changes no availability decisions and changes matched covariance by at most 4.86e-7.

This study tests a specified full-system HC3-style correction and actual whole-person delete-one refitting on fresh random-number streams. It is a 600-dataset exploratory validation screen: six profiles × 100 new measurement datasets, each with paired null and nonzero structural outcomes. Its purpose is to distinguish uncertainty propagation, leverage adjustment, refitting, interval construction, bias and numerical availability. It does not select a correction by maximizing observed coverage or claim uniform validity.

The numerical implementation and protocol were frozen before main results. Earlier experiments remain unchanged. All methods retain the original REPAIR point estimate; neither jackknife bias nor a simulation-estimated bias is subtracted from the interval center.

The design retains the earlier noisy-predictor experiment: within-person time is centered and sample-SD standardized; measurement Y=.5time+b0+b1time+eps; random intercept/slope SDs .9 and correlation +/−.5; Gaussian iid measurement errors calibrated to full-posterior slope reliability .25 or .8. The unequal profile assigns half the people to 3 and half to 17 observations independently of latent effects/errors.

The structural outcome is Z=1.5+.4b0+(gamma/.9)b1+eta, with Var(Z)=1, Gaussian homoskedastic eta and gamma=0/.40. Both recovered intercept and slope enter as noisy predictors. All focal coefficients, SEs and endpoints are multiplied by population SD .9. Gamma=0 is a null partial slope given the other noisy random coefficient, not necessarily a null marginal association.

New L’Ecuyer-CMRG master seed 202610319 replaces the old 202610301; bootstrap seed is 340000000+replication. Independent outer streams are paired across profiles, and null/effect outcomes share measurement data/noise. This gives 1,200 structural analyses, not 1,200 independent measurement datasets. The validation checks fresh input hashes against every old main-study input.

Main uses B499. The first three datasets/profile extend to B1999 and halve the analytic derivative step; no subset was chosen by its results. Development replication 801/B9 is excluded. No failed dataset is regenerated or replaced.

What the methods estimate

Conditional Wald retains ordinary model-based M-MOM SEs. Full IF Wald uses the existing complete influence-function sandwich, including measurement estimation, structural weights/corrections and signed cross-stage covariance. Both full-system methods use exact ML/REML measurement equations, with the global REML fixed-design determinant retained. No ML scores at a REML fit are substituted.

Full-system HC3 Wald augments measurement parameters with unweighted observed/ error moments, weighted observed/error moments, log mean case weight and final corrected coefficient equations. All preliminary coefficients, variance floors, weights and correction multipliers are differentiated. Known error-free entries remain fixed. The mean-weight equation normalizes the final coefficient equation, cancelling an irrelevant common weight in OLS. That normalization was specified during pre-main development after an OLS acceptance test detected a spurious common-weight leverage effect.

For each person, solve the deleted augmented system’s Jacobian at the original parameters, using the exact deleted REML determinant. Sum uncentered outer products of the resulting coefficient shifts. This recovers ordinary OLS HC3 in the matching special case. No measurement model is refitted. Original N and policy/alpha remain fixed in this analytic structural correction. All deleted systems and the original full influence must be usable; failures are never silently replaced by HC0 or omitted. Sensitivities are centrally differentiated with half-step, one-sided and active-branch checks and scaled conditioning gates.

This is an explicitly specified HC3-style nonlinear-system candidate; leverage adjustments depend on the equation representation. It is not a derived CR2/Satterthwaite procedure or a theorem of nominal finite-sample coverage. The full derivation is in dev/leverage-jackknife-design.md in the PR. The OLS anchor and augmented HC0/canonical IF identity check validate implementation, not a general finite-sample approximation theorem.

Delete-one Wald refits each measurement and structural model on N-1 complete people, updating all finite-N corrections and weights. Its variance is (N-1)/N times the centered delete-one cross-product. Every complete coefficient vector is required; a failed deletion invalidates inference. Singular but converged native refits retain the existing replay policy and are recorded. Diagnostic jackknife bias is not subtracted. The analytic and actual deletion methods therefore differ in nonlinear re-estimation, finite-N updates, and HC3 versus centered jackknife scaling.

Person percentile samples N complete people and fully refits measurement and structural models, using the original complete-vector failure gate and type-7 percentile endpoints. Bootstrap-SD Wald instead uses the SD of those same bootstrap coefficients in a normal symmetric interval; it is not a percentile-t bootstrap. Frozen-measurement percentile and stage2 IF are diagnostic comparators. The unequal profile additionally retains a count-preserving stratified comparator. The earlier OLS-outcome stacked helper is not applied to this incompatible noisy- predictor estimand; OLS HC3 is checked independently in package tests.

Normal reference intervals are primary. HC3 and delete-one t_(N−1) intervals are prespecified secondary heuristics, not fitted effective degrees of freedom. There is no data-selected multiplier or hidden finite-sample correction.

Bias and the sampling-error distribution

All methods retain the same original coefficient, so separate method-specific bias curves would duplicate the point estimator. This figure uses all 100 fresh datasets per profile and truth, showing each signed estimation error and mean bias with its Monte Carlo uncertainty. It makes the negative bias in the small/short and negative-correlation conditions visible alongside the distribution’s tails. The blue error bars concern the simulation mean bias; they are not the confidence intervals whose coverage is assessed below.

Bias conditional on returning an interval can differ because eligibility selects different datasets; those eligible-set summaries remain in performance.csv.

Analytic inference refuses singular/weakly identified original measurement fits and unstable or weak deleted sensitivities. Actual refitting can remain usable at singular native covariances; that difference is explicit, not an error hidden by denominator changes. Every analytic refusal and native deletion failure is archived. Coverage and zero exclusion below use available intervals only; performance.csv also reports delivery-and-cover/detect per all 100 planned data. Unavailable intervals remain NA, never valid non-rejections.

Tail behavior: wide intervals and studentized errors

The width axis is logarithmic so typical intervals and extreme corrections remain visible together. Circles show medians, diamonds empirical 95th percentiles, and triangles the largest observed intervals. The full-system HC3 tail is much longer in the difficult profiles; the typical-width summary alone conceals that cost. Every returned interval contributes, and the maximum is never dropped or winsorized. These are empirical summaries from 45–100 returned intervals per cell, not precise estimates of population-tail quantiles.

The step curves show the fraction of returned intervals wider than each threshold, focusing vertically on the upper 20% of widths. All observed thresholds remain on the logarithmic horizontal axis, and each curve reaches zero at its observed maximum. The horizontal 5% line helps locate the upper tail; finite-sample step locations need not equal interpolated type-7 quantiles exactly. Eligibility still differs here; the denominators are those shown in the method-specific coverage figures.

This diagnostic instead uses the same all-five-method eligibility cohort and compares absolute errors divided by estimated SEs. The black dashed curve is the standard-normal benchmark. At 1.96, a calibrated normal Wald procedure would have about 5% exceedance; departures show that estimating a variance is not enough to establish normal tail calibration. The upper 25% of this error distribution is displayed, retaining all observed horizontal thresholds with log(1+x) spacing. Bootstrap SD is the symmetric Wald comparator, not the bootstrap percentile interval; a percentile interval cannot be diagnosed by assuming its resample SD defines a symmetric normal interval.

The relative RMSE divides the sum of squared analytic-minus-actual shifts by the sum of squared actual shifts (with a small numerical floor). A discrepancy can reflect curvature, branch changes, finite-N policy updates and centering/ scaling conventions; it is not automatically an implementation error. HC0 identity and OLS HC3 tests provide independent implementation anchors.

Availability changes under half steps and matched covariance differences are reported without choosing the better-performing step. The B1999 subset retains exact B499 prefixes; endpoint/availability changes are archived in bootstrap_sensitivity.csv. This small tail subset is not a high-precision coverage experiment.

All 78 fixed-subset percentile intervals were available at B499; six become unavailable at B1999 under the unchanged all-vector failure rule. Among the 72 returned at both B values, coverage classification is unchanged (all cover). Median sums of absolute lower/upper endpoint changes are .0246 for person percentile, .0310 frozen, and .0326 stratified. The sensitivity comparison preserves those lost intervals; it does not silently condition the primary analysis on successes or replace failures with new draws.

A separate post hoc numerical audit, motivated by the unusually wide tails, checked the 12 largest HC3/HC0 variance ratios at h/2 and h/4. All 24 comparisons remained available; the largest relative full-covariance change was 1.06e-4 (about .011%). This supports treating the large corrections as properties of the specified approximation rather than gross differencing error. It is not a prespecified coverage comparison or proof of exact numerical precision. No main estimate, step, threshold or interval was replaced. The rule and outputs are retained in audit_extremes.R and posthoc_extreme_audit.csv.

The computational shortcut caches immutable individual OLS/design-inverse ingredients for this iid matching-design DGP. Every bootstrap and delete-one measurement model is actually optimized, with its fixed coefficients/sigma and all structural equations updated. Eligibility requires full coefficient vectors, not just a finite focal slope. Fixed subsets are verified against 24 complete public B99 bootstraps and 12 complete public jackknives. No failed vector is replaced, trimmed or silently accepted.

Reproducibility and limits

Numerical baseline is repair cbffe31, built on PR #21 head 6bb14dc. Subsequent documentation and an explicit utils::tail qualification preserve the equations; the frozen installed simulation library is not overwritten. The protocol, drivers, source/library/reference hashes, sessions and full native histories are retained in the research workspace’s leverage_fresh directory. The PR’s dev/leverage-simulation bundle permits independent endpoint/rate verification without fitting hundreds of thousands of models. Its README explains the external research-source dependencies and distinguishes compact review evidence from a complete raw optimization archive.

These results cover Gaussian iid measurement errors, six fixed reliability/ schedule conditions and a particular noisy-predictor structural design. They do not validate informative missingness, misspecification, shared nuisance effects, multiple measurement models or uniform boundary coverage. Neither a finite interval nor an exact covariance decomposition establishes calibrated inference; point bias, width, power and availability remain part of the assessment.

The package therefore retains both new methods as opt-in experimental tools. The leverage result is useful for inspecting the complete system’s sensitivity; actual delete-one refits provide a complementary influence/branch diagnostic. These results do not support making either symmetric interval the default solution for weak noisy predictors. Bootstrap likewise remains imperfect, especially with short panels and boundary/convergence issues.
